a: Ananias the high priest
p: High priest about AD 47 to 59, remembered by Josephus for greed and violence, and killed by rebels in 66.
b: This is the Ananias who had Paul struck on the mouth (23:2), not the Ananias of 5:1 or 9:10. Josephus calls him Ananias son of Nedebaeus. He says Ananias' servants went to the threshing floors and took by force the tithes meant for ordinary priests, so that some poor priests starved (Antiquities 20.205–207). Ananias stayed powerful after he lost the office, but when the revolt against Rome broke out in AD 66 the rebels found him hiding in an aqueduct and killed him (Jewish War 2.441). That the high priest himself made the 60-mile trip to Caesarea shows how seriously the Temple leaders took Paul's case.

a: an advocate, a certain Tertullus
p: Rhētōr means a trained public speaker, the kind of advocate a party hired for a Roman court.
b: The Greek rhētōr is a speaker trained in rhetoric, the art every educated Greek and Roman studied. In a provincial court the parties often hired one to plead for them. Tertullus is a Latin name, and he may have been chosen because he knew Roman procedure. Whether he was a Jew is not clear. He says "we" in 24:6, but an advocate spoke in the person of his clients. Luke gives his speech in a few lines, but they follow the textbook pattern: praise of the judge, a promise to be brief, the charges, and an appeal to the judge to check for himself.

a: your foresight
p: Tertullus praises Felix for peace and foresight. Josephus and Tacitus remember Felix differently.
b: "Foresight" (pronoia, Latin providentia) was a virtue Roman rulers advertised on coins and inscriptions. Speeches to a judge customarily opened with praise of this kind. The "great peace" was half true. Felix did hunt down bandits and false prophets, among them the followers of the Egyptian (21:38), whom his troops cut down (Josephus, Jewish War 2.253–263). But Josephus also says Felix had the former high priest Jonathan murdered (Antiquities 20.162–164), and his rule saw the rise of the sicarii, the dagger men. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote that Felix "used the power of a king with the mind of a slave" (Histories 5.9). Readers who knew this would hear the flattery as hollow.

a: most excellent Felix
p: The courtesy title for Roman officials of the equestrian class, the same one Luke gives Theophilus.
b: Kratistos, "most excellent," translated the Latin egregius, the title of men of the equestrian order, Rome's second rank. Lysias uses it of Felix (23:26), Paul uses it of Festus (26:25), and Luke uses it of Theophilus (Luke 1:3). Felix had in fact been born a slave. He was a freedman of the emperor's family and the brother of Pallas, Claudius' powerful finance secretary, which is how he rose so far (Tacitus, Annals 12.54; Histories 5.9). The title marks him as a man who had arrived.

a: a pest
p: The charge is not heresy but public disorder, the one thing a Roman governor could not ignore.
b: Loimos means "plague, pestilence": a man who spreads trouble like a disease. The real charge follows: he "starts uprisings" (staseis, the word for civil unrest and rebellion) "across the empire" (oikoumenē, the inhabited world, which to a Roman meant the empire). That framed Paul as a threat to Roman order. The language sounds like the emperor Claudius' letter to the Alexandrians in AD 41, which warned the Jews of Alexandria not to bring in other Jews from Syria and Egypt, or he would treat them as "stirring up a common plague for the whole world" (London Papyrus 1912). Tertullus knows what Rome feared. Luke's readers knew that the same word for uprising was used of Barabbas (Luke 23:19, 25).

a: the sect of the Nazarenes
p: The only place the New Testament calls Jesus' followers Nazarenes. Jews and Arabs still call Christians by this name.
b: Jesus is often called "the Nazarene" (2:22; 26:9), but only here are his followers called Nazōraioi. The name lasted outside the church: in Hebrew Christians are Notsrim, in Arabic Nasara. Some medieval copies of the synagogue's Eighteen Blessings found in the Cairo Genizah curse "the Notsrim" alongside heretics. Epiphanius (about 375) describes a group of Jewish believers called Nazoraeans who kept the Law (Panarion 29). "Sect" (hairesis) is not an insult in itself: Luke uses it for the Sadducees (5:17) and the Pharisees (15:5; 26:5). It means a party or school within Judaism, and that is how Tertullus places the movement.

a: make the temple unholy
p: Bringing a Gentile past the barrier was a crime Rome let the Jewish authorities punish by death.
b: The charge goes back to 21:28–29, where Jews from Asia claimed Paul had taken Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, into the inner courts. Warning stones on the barrier said that a foreigner who passed it would have himself to blame for his death (see 21:28). Josephus has Titus remind the rebels that Rome had allowed them to execute even Roman citizens for this offense (Jewish War 6.124–126). So this was the one charge on which the priests might claim the right to try Paul themselves. That is why Tertullus says they "took hold of him," and why, in the longer text, he complains that Lysias took him away (see the variant at 24:7).

a: for many years
p: Felix governed Judea from about AD 52. Tacitus suggests he held power in Samaria even earlier.
b: Josephus has Claudius send Felix as governor after Cumanus was recalled, about AD 52. Tacitus says that Felix had already ruled Samaria while Cumanus ruled Galilee (Annals 12.54), which would stretch his years in the region back toward 48. Either way, by Paul's trial he had served six years or more, a long time for a governor. Paul's opening is courteous but restrained beside Tertullus' flattery: he praises nothing but Felix's experience, which means Felix should be able to see through the charges.

a: no more than twelve days
p: Too short a visit to organize a revolt. Commentators count the days in different ways.
b: Paul's point is that he had not been in Jerusalem long enough to stir up anything, and that he had come to worship. Commentators add up the days from 21:17 to 24:1 in several ways (the seven days of purification in 21:27, the day before the council in 22:30, the night journey in 23:23–32, the five days in 24:1), and the total depends on whether the time in Caesarea counts. The number fits the story roughly; it is a courtroom claim, not a calendar.

a: the Way
p: The earliest name the believers used for themselves in Acts. Qumran used "the way" for its life too.
b: Hē hodos, "the Way," is Acts' name for the movement (9:2; 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:22). It may come from the prophet's cry, "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3), which the Gospels apply to John the Baptist. The community of the Dead Sea Scrolls used the same verse and called its life in the wilderness "the way" (Community Rule, 1QS 8:13–16; 9:17–20). For Jews, a "way" was also how one walked with God, the root idea of halakhah, the path of practice. Paul accepts the name "Way" and rejects "sect" in the sense of a split-off group: this is how he serves the God of his ancestors.

a: which they call a sect
p: The KJV says "heresy" here but "sect" in 24:5. Hairesis meant a party, not a false teaching.
b: The King James Version renders this verse "after the way which they call heresy," though it translates the same Greek word "sect" in 24:5, 26:5 and 28:22. In the first century hairesis meant "choice," then a school or party: Josephus uses it for the Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes. The sense "false teaching" came later, through letters like 2 Peter 2:1 and the church fathers. Modern readers of the KJV can hear Paul admitting to heresy. What he is doing is objecting to being called a breakaway party at all.

a: our ancestors' God
p: Paul claims continuity: he worships the same God as every Jew, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
b: The Greek is "the ancestral God" (tō patrōō theō), the God of the fathers. In the burning bush God names himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob" (Exodus 3:6), and Peter used that name in the temple (3:13). Paul's defense rests on this: the Way is not a new religion but faithfulness to Israel's God, his Law and his Prophets. Jewish scholars such as Alan Segal and Paula Fredriksen have taken that claim seriously: Paul never thought of himself as leaving Judaism.

a: of the righteous and the unrighteous alike
p: The only place Paul speaks of the unrighteous being raised too. Jews of his day disagreed about it.
b: Daniel 12:2 had foreseen many who sleep in the dust waking, some to life without end and some to shame and horror without end. Some Jewish writings expected everyone to rise for judgment (1 Enoch 51:1; 4 Ezra 7:32–37). Others spoke only of the righteous rising. Josephus says the Pharisees taught that good souls pass into another body while the wicked suffer eternal punishment (Jewish War 2.163), which sounds like a resurrection for the good alone. Jesus in John 5:28–29 speaks of two outcomes. Paul's letters speak almost only of believers' resurrection (1 Corinthians 15; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Christians later drew different conclusions from this verse; see the card on this chapter.

a: keeping my conscience free of blame
p: Syneidēsis, a Greek word Paul uses often in his letters. Acts has it only here and at 23:1.
b: Syneidēsis is the inner knowledge that judges one's own actions. The word has no exact Hebrew equivalent; the Old Testament speaks of the heart. Paul uses it many times in his letters (Romans 2:15; 1 Corinthians 8:7–12; 2 Corinthians 1:12). "Free of blame" is aproskopos, "not stumbling" or "not making others stumble," a word Paul also uses (1 Corinthians 10:32; Philippians 1:10). "I work hard" (askō) is the language of athletic training, the root of English "ascetic."

a: to give alms for my people
p: Paul's letters say he came to Jerusalem with a large gift from his churches. Acts mentions it only here.
b: For years Paul had gathered money from the churches of Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–28; compare Galatians 2:10). He saw it as a sign that Gentile and Jewish believers were one. He feared it might not be accepted (Romans 15:31). Acts, which tells of the trip in detail, never says what became of the gift; this half sentence is the only trace. Some scholars think the Jerusalem church refused it, or took it only on conditions such as Paul's vow in 21:23–26, and that Luke kept quiet. Others think "alms" here means something else. The silence is real and unexplained.

a: to present offerings
p: Paul says he came to offer sacrifices in the temple. Acts presents him as a Jew who keeps the Law.
b: "Offerings" (prosphorai) are temple sacrifices. They fit the vow of 21:23–26, where James asked Paul to pay for the sacrifices of four men ending a Nazirite vow and to purify himself with them (Numbers 6:13–20). Many Christians are surprised to read that Paul brought offerings after the death of Jesus. Jacob Jervell argued that this is exactly Luke's point: Paul is the faithful Pharisee, "the Jew" among Jews, and the charges that he taught Jews to abandon Moses (21:21) are false. Others think Luke has smoothed over real tensions visible in Paul's letters (Galatians 2:11–14).

a: some Jews from Asia
p: Paul's sentence breaks off. His real point: the eyewitnesses who started the riot have not come.
b: The Greek sentence starts with "some Jews from Asia" and never finishes it; Paul turns to a new thought. The Jews from the province of Asia were the ones who saw Paul in the temple and raised the cry (21:27). Roman law expected accusers to appear in person, and it penalized those who brought a charge and then dropped it; a few years later, in AD 61, a decree of the Senate (the senatus consultum Turpillianum) tightened those penalties. Paul's point is legal and sharp: the only witnesses to the alleged crime are absent, so there is no case.

a: except for one sentence
p: Paul refers back to his cry in the council that he was on trial over the resurrection of the dead.
b: In 23:6 Paul cried out in the council that he was on trial over the hope of the resurrection, and the Pharisees and Sadducees fell to fighting. Now he offers that cry as his only "crime." There is a little irony in it: the cry had been shrewd, and it split the court. It also sets the theme for the rest of Acts. In every hearing from here on, before Felix, Festus (25:19) and Agrippa (26:6–8, 23), Paul says the real question is the resurrection.

a: quite accurate knowledge about the Way
p: Caesarea had believers from early on, and Felix's wife was Jewish. He knew enough to stall.
b: Luke does not say how Felix knew about the Way. Believers had lived in Caesarea since Philip settled there and Cornelius was baptized (8:40; 10:1–48; 21:8), and Felix's wife Drusilla came from the Herod family (24:24). Felix promises to decide when Lysias comes, but Lysias' letter had already given his view (23:26–30), and Luke never mentions him again. The delay was a decision not to decide. It kept the priests from losing face and left Felix free to see what Paul might be worth to him (24:26).

a: to let him have some relief
p: Roman custody came in grades. Paul was held by soldiers but could receive visitors and food.
b: Rome did not use prison as a sentence. It held people until trial, in conditions that ranged from a dark cell to living at home with a soldier. Status mattered: Paul was a Roman citizen and accused of no proven crime, so he got "relief" (anesis), and his "own people" could bring food and care. Brian Rapske has shown how much prisoners relied on friends for food, clothing and visits. Paul spent two years like this in Herod's palace in Caesarea (23:35). Some scholars think Luke used the time, when the "we" falls silent, to gather material for his Gospel (Luke 1:1–3); that is a guess, but a reasonable one.

a: Drusilla, his own wife, a Jewish woman
p: Youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. Felix had lured her away from her first husband, a king.
b: Drusilla was the daughter of Herod Agrippa I, whose death Acts tells in 12:20–23, and the sister of Agrippa II and Bernice (25:13). Josephus says she was married to Azizus, king of Emesa, who was circumcised for her. Felix fell for her and, through a Jewish friend from Cyprus who posed as a magician, persuaded her to leave her husband and marry him, against the Law. She was perhaps twenty. Their son Agrippa died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 (Antiquities 20.141–144). Suetonius calls Felix "the husband of three queens" (Claudius 28). This helps explain why talk of self-control frightened him (24:25).

a: righteousness, about self-control and about the judgment that lies ahead
p: Justice, self-control and judgment: the three points touch Felix's rule, his marriage, and his future.
b: Dikaiosynē is "righteousness," but to a Roman governor it also meant "justice," the duty of a judge. Enkrateia, "self-control," was a virtue every philosopher praised, and Felix had taken another man's wife. "The judgment that lies ahead" put the judge himself on trial before God. Felix asked to hear about "faith in Christ Jesus" (24:24), and Paul told him what faith demands. The King James words "when I have a convenient season" became a byword in English preaching for putting off a decision about God.
orig: δικαιοσύνης, ἐγκρατείας, κρίματος τοῦ μέλλοντος (dikaiosynēs, enkrateias, krimatos tou mellontos)

a: He was also hoping, all the while
p: Roman law forbade officials to take money to free a prisoner. Governors did it anyway.
b: Laws against extortion by officials (the lex Julia de repetundis) forbade a governor to take money to release or condemn anyone. Josephus says that a later governor, Albinus, emptied the prisons by letting out anyone whose family paid (Antiquities 20.215; Jewish War 2.273). Felix may have thought Paul had money: he had just spoken of bringing alms to Jerusalem (24:17), and he had friends who visited him (24:23). The Byzantine text and the KJV add "that he might loose him" (see the variant). Paul paid nothing, and he stayed.

a: Two full years went by
t: Two years, and a new governor
p: Most date Festus' arrival to about AD 59 or 60, though some argue for a date as early as 55 or 56.
b: "Two years" most likely means Paul's time in custody, though some read it as Felix's term. Josephus says Felix was recalled after the Jews of Caesarea accused him, and that his brother Pallas saved him (Antiquities 20.182). Since Pallas lost his post in 55 (Tacitus, Annals 13.14), a few scholars move Festus' arrival early. Most prefer AD 59 or 60, which fits Josephus' order of events and Festus' death in office around 62. This date is a fixed point for Paul's chronology. Some later manuscripts (614 and the margin of the Harclean Syriac, reported by Metzger) say Felix left Paul in custody "because of Drusilla."

a: store up favor with the Jews
p: The Greek pictures depositing goodwill like money, to draw on later. Festus does the same in 25:9.
b: Charita katathesthai means "to lay down a favor" as one deposits money. A departing governor facing complaints in Rome had good reason to leave the Temple leaders in his debt. The same phrase returns with Festus (25:9). Luke's Roman officials are often fair-minded, but he does not hide how politics bent their justice. Pilate too released Barabbas to please the crowd (Luke 23:24–25).

a: Festus took up his post in the province
p: Governor about AD 59 to 62. Josephus remembers him as firmer than Felix. His death opened the way for the killing of James.
b: Josephus says Festus found the countryside full of bandits and the sicarii, and moved against them and against a false prophet who led people into the desert (Antiquities 20.185–188; Jewish War 2.271). He also had to settle a quarrel between Agrippa II and the priests over a wall that blocked the king's view into the temple courts (Antiquities 20.189–196). Festus died in office about 62. Before his successor Albinus arrived, the high priest Ananus had James, "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ," stoned (Antiquities 20.197–203). That James is the leader Paul met in 21:18. A new governor going up to Jerusalem within three days shows how much the province depended on the Temple leadership.

a: They were setting a trap to kill him on the road
p: Two years after the first plot (23:12–22), the same plan returns. Luke draws the parallel on purpose.
b: In 23:12–22 more than forty men swore not to eat until they had killed Paul, and his nephew warned the commander. Now the leaders ask for a transfer so that Paul can be killed on the road. Luke repeats the danger to show that Paul's appeal to Caesar in 25:11 was not a stunt but the only safe road left. Readers who knew Jesus' story would recall that he too was taken from one ruler to another (Luke 23:6–12).

a: sat on the judgment seat
p: The raised platform where a Roman magistrate sat to give binding rulings. Paul calls it "Caesar's."
b: The bēma was a raised platform in a public place where a magistrate sat to hear cases. A decision given from it was official. Gallio's bēma still stands in the forum of Corinth (18:12), and Pilate sat on one (Matthew 27:19; John 19:13). Paul uses the same word for the judgment of God (Romans 14:10; 2 Corinthians 5:10). When Festus takes his seat the day after he arrives, the hearing becomes a formal Roman trial, and that is why Paul can say in 25:10 that he is already standing at Caesar's judgment seat.

a: not against the Jews' law, not against the temple, and not against Caesar
p: Religious law, the temple, and the emperor: only the last made a case for Roman courts.
b: Paul's denial names the three kinds of charge his enemies had made. Breaking the Jewish law was not a Roman crime. Defiling the temple was a capital matter that Rome let the Jewish authorities judge (see 24:6). An offense "against Caesar" meant treason or sedition (Latin maiestas), the charge Tertullus hinted at when he said Paul "starts uprisings among all the Jews across the empire" (24:5). The same mix had been aimed at Jesus, who was accused before Pilate of forbidding taxes to Caesar (Luke 23:2). A governor had to take the third seriously, and Paul's opponents knew it.

a: I am standing at Caesar's judgment seat
p: A trial in Jerusalem "in front of me" sounded fair. Paul saw that it meant being handed to his enemies.
b: Festus offers to hear the case in Jerusalem himself. But the Jerusalem setting would hand the advantage to the priests, who could argue that a temple offense belonged to their own court, and the road there had already been planned as a trap (25:3). A Roman citizen had the right to be tried by Roman law. Paul's reply is blunt: he is already before Caesar's representative, and Festus knows the charges are empty. To a Roman official such directness was risky, but it was within Paul's rights.

a: I appeal to Caesar!
p: A Roman citizen could ask to be judged by the emperor himself. Paul's appeal moves his case to Rome.
b: Roman citizens had long had the right of provocatio, an appeal to the people against a magistrate's power over life and body; under the emperors this became an appeal to Caesar. The Julian law on public violence forbade officials to kill, flog or torture a citizen who had appealed. Paul appeals before any verdict, which fits the older right as A. N. Sherwin-White described it for the 50s and 60s. Later governors judged more citizens themselves; but Pliny, about 112, still sent Christians who were Roman citizens to Rome (Letters 10.96). The emperor was Nero, then in the early years of his reign, which Romans remembered as good. Paul's appeal also brings about what the Lord had promised in 23:11.

a: I am not trying to get out of dying
p: Paul grants that some crimes deserve death. Christians on both sides of the death penalty debate cite him.
b: Paul does not say Rome has no right to execute; he says he has done nothing that deserves it. Defenders of capital punishment have often pointed to this verse, together with Romans 13:4 (the ruler "does not carry the sword for nothing"), to show that the apostles accepted it as the state's right. Others answer that Paul is simply speaking inside the law of his time, as a defendant would, and that the verse says nothing about whether Christians should support the death penalty. The Catholic Church, for example, now teaches that it is inadmissible (Catechism 2267, revised 2018), without denying this verse.

a: make a gift of me to them
p: The verb charizomai means to grant as a favor. Luke uses it for a life handed over, and a life given back.
b: Charizomai comes from charis, "grace, favor." Paul means that Festus cannot hand him over as a favor to the Jews. Festus himself uses the word in 25:16. Luke has used it before: the crowd in Jerusalem asked for a murderer "to be granted" to them instead of Jesus (3:14). And Luke will use it again in the storm, when an angel tells Paul that God "has made you a gift of everyone who is sailing with you" (27:24). Rulers trade lives as favors; God gives lives as gifts.

a: his advisers
p: Not the Jewish Sanhedrin but the circle of officers and friends a Roman magistrate consulted.
b: Symboulion here is the governor's consilium: the advisers, junior officials and friends a Roman magistrate called in before giving a ruling. Its advice did not bind him, but consulting it was expected. The question was not whether Paul could appeal (that was his right) but whether the case was one Festus had to send on. They decided that it was.

a: King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice
p: The last of the Herod kings and his sister. Rome trusted him with the temple and its high priests.
b: Marcus Julius Agrippa (Agrippa II) was the son of the Herod who killed James and died in 12:20–23. Rome gave him lands north and east of Galilee, the care of the temple and the right to appoint high priests. Bernice was his sister, widow of their uncle Herod of Chalcis, and often at his side; gossip said they were lovers (Josephus, Antiquities 20.145; Juvenal, Satires 6.156–160). Years later she lived openly with Titus, the general who destroyed Jerusalem, until Roman opinion forced him to send her away (Tacitus, Histories 2.2; Suetonius, Titus 7). In 66 Agrippa pleaded with Jerusalem not to revolt (Jewish War 2.345–404), then fought on Rome's side.

a: face to face
p: Festus tells Agrippa he defended Roman fairness. Luke has just shown him offering Paul to Jerusalem.
b: The rule Festus states was real Roman practice: the accused must meet his accusers and have the chance to answer them, a principle the Roman law books later set down and Trajan repeated against anonymous charges (Pliny, Letters 10.97). But readers have just watched Festus ask Paul to go to Jerusalem to please the priests (25:9), and they will notice that in his report the favor-seeking has vanished. Luke lets officials tell their own stories and trusts the reader to compare, as he did with Lysias' letter (23:27).

a: their own religion
p: Deisidaimonia can mean reverence for the gods or fear of them. Festus may be polite, or he may sneer.
b: Deisidaimonia literally means "fear of the divine beings." It could be a neutral word for religion, and Festus is talking to a Jewish king, so he may be careful. But Greek writers such as Plutarch used it for anxious superstition. Paul used the related adjective at Athens, where it is also hard to tell praise from irony (17:22). Either way, to Festus the dispute is an internal Jewish matter of belief, not a crime, much as it was to Gallio (18:14–15) and Lysias (23:29).

a: one Jesus, who had died, and who Paul kept saying is alive
t: The gospel in a governor's words
p: An outsider's one-line summary of Christian faith: a dead man named Jesus whom Paul says is alive.
b: Festus has the essentials right without believing them. "He is alive" is how the angels at the tomb put it (Luke 24:5, 23), and Acts opens with Jesus showing himself "alive" after his suffering (1:3). Luke liked to put the message in the mouths of outsiders: the Philippian slave girl (16:17), the Athenian philosophers (17:18), and now a Roman governor. To Festus the claim is so strange that he cannot judge it, which is exactly why he does not know what to write to Rome (25:26).

a: the emperor
p: The Greek is Sebastos, "the revered one," the Greek form of the title Augustus. The KJV keeps "Augustus."
b: In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus, "revered, sacred," and every emperor after him bore it. In Greek it was Sebastos, the word behind the city name Sebaste (Samaria) and the "Emperor's Cohort" of 27:1. The emperor here is Nero (54–68). The KJV prints "Augustus" (25:21, 25), which leads some readers to think of the first emperor, who died in AD 14. A title that meant "worthy of worship" was one reason Christians came into conflict with the cult of the emperor.

a: in grand display
p: Phantasia means show, parade. Luke sets a royal procession beside a man in chains.
b: Phantasia is "appearance, display," the root of English "fantasy." Agrippa and Bernice enter in state with the five commanders of the Caesarea garrison (each over a cohort) and the city's leading men. The setting is the same city where their father, Agrippa I, put on royal robes, let the crowd hail his voice as a god's, and was struck down (12:20–23). Luke does not underline the irony. Jesus had told his followers they would be "taken before governors and kings" (Matthew 10:18), and Paul's call promised he would carry the name "before Gentiles, before kings" (9:15). Here it happens.

a: he had done nothing that deserves death
p: Every Roman who hears Paul finds him innocent. Luke told Jesus' trial the same way.
b: Lysias found no charge that deserved death or chains (23:29); Festus finds nothing worthy of death; Agrippa and the others will agree (26:31–32). In Luke's Gospel Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times (Luke 23:4, 14, 22), and Herod Antipas agrees (Luke 23:15). The parallel is deliberate: Paul follows his Lord through Jerusalem, a Roman governor and a Herod, and in both stories the officials see the innocence and still do not let the man go. For Luke's readers, often accused of disloyalty to Rome, this was also a defense: Roman judges had found nothing against the faith.

a: our lord
p: Kyrios, "lord," for the emperor. Augustus had refused the title. By Nero's day it was common in the East.
b: Festus calls the emperor simply "the lord" (ho kyrios). Augustus and Tiberius had refused the Latin dominus, "master," as a title for themselves (Suetonius, Augustus 53; Tiberius 27), but in the Greek East "lord" was used for emperors by Nero's time, and Domitian later wanted to be called "lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13). Christians confessed "Jesus is Lord" (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), the same word. In the second century, Polycarp of Smyrna was urged to save his life by saying "Lord Caesar," and refused.

a: I may have something to write
p: An appealed case went to Rome with the governor's written report. Festus had nothing to put in it.
b: When a case was sent up on appeal, the magistrate sent a letter explaining it (later law calls such letters litterae dimissoriae). Festus faces an awkward problem: he has a prisoner whose accusers want him dead and no charge that a Roman court would recognize. Agrippa, an expert in Jewish matters (26:3), is his way out. The hearing that follows is not a trial but an inquiry, held to help Festus write his letter.

a: Paul held out his hand
p: Paul begins like a trained speaker. This is the most polished speech in Acts.
b: Speakers in the Greek and Roman world opened by stretching out the right hand, a gesture the rhetoric handbooks describe. The speech that follows is the most carefully built in Acts: a courteous opening (26:2–3), Paul's early life (26:4–11), his call (26:12–18), his obedience (26:19–23), and an appeal to the king (26:27). Its Greek is the most literary in the book, with classical forms such as isasi, "they know" (26:4), and the superlative akribestatēn, "most exacting" (26:5). Luke dresses Paul for the most distinguished audience of his life. Whether the speech gives Paul's words or Luke's summary of them is the old question about all the speeches in Acts (see the chapter page).

a: you know well every custom and every debate among the Jews
p: Agrippa II controlled the temple's high priesthood and its robes. He really did know Jewish law.
b: Rome entrusted Agrippa II with the temple: he appointed and removed high priests (Josephus names several he chose) and kept the high priest's robes. He also built a dining room on his palace from which he could watch the sacrifices, and the priests answered by building a wall to block his view; Festus and Nero were drawn into the quarrel (Antiquities 20.189–196). So Paul's praise is accurate. It also sets up the end of the speech: a king who knows the Prophets (26:27) should be able to judge whether Paul's message agrees with them.

a: I lived as a Pharisee
p: Paul calls the Pharisees the strictest party, the very word Josephus uses for their exactness.
b: "Most exacting" is akribestatē, from akribeia, "precision, strictness." Josephus, himself a Pharisee in public life, says the Pharisees were reputed to interpret the laws with the most exactness (Jewish War 1.110; 2.162; Life 191). Paul says the same of himself in his letters: "When it came to the law, I was a Pharisee" (Philippians 3:5), "far more zealous for the traditions of my fathers" (Galatians 1:14). In Acts he still calls himself a Pharisee in the present tense (23:6). Jewish scholars such as Alan Segal have used Paul as the only Pharisee before AD 70 whose own writings survive.
orig: κατὰ τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν (kata tēn akribestatēn hairesin)

a: Our twelve tribes
p: One Greek word: "the twelve-tribe nation." Paul speaks as if all twelve still exist and still hope.
b: To dōdekaphylon is a single word, "the twelve-tribe people," Israel as a whole. Paul does not speak of ten lost tribes; for him the whole people, wherever its members live, still waits for God's promise. James addresses "the twelve tribes in the dispersion" (James 1:1), and Luke's Gospel includes Anna of the tribe of Asher, who served in the temple "night and day" (Luke 2:36–37), the same phrase Paul uses here. The hope of the promise, for Paul, is the hope that God raises the dead and fulfills his word to the fathers, and he insists that this is Israel's own hope (28:20).

a: God raises dead people
p: Paul turns from Agrippa to everyone present. Jews prayed daily to God "who gives life to the dead."
b: The "you" is plural: Paul turns to the whole hall, Romans included. To Greek and Roman ears the raising of a body was absurd (17:32), and Festus will soon call Paul mad. But for Jews it was part of daily prayer: the second blessing of the Amidah praises God who "gives life to the dead." The Song of Moses has God say, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Paul's question asks his Jewish hearers why they should balk at a hope their own Scriptures and prayers already hold.

a: I added my vote against them
p: Literally "I cast down my pebble." Was Paul a voting member of a court, or is this a figure for approving?
b: Voters in Greek courts cast pebbles (psēphoi), and "to cast a pebble" meant "to vote." Taken literally, Paul sat on a court that sentenced believers to death, which some take to mean he was a member of the Sanhedrin or of a smaller court. Against that, Acts calls him a "young man" at Stephen's death (7:58), and the Sanhedrin's members were usually older. Many think the phrase is a figure: Paul approved the killings (8:1; 22:20). Acts names only one death, Stephen's, though "when they were being executed" suggests more. Paul's own letters say he "persecuted the church of God beyond all measure" and was "trying to wreck it" (Galatians 1:13).

a: the saints
p: Hagioi, "holy ones," is what the first believers called each other. Every believer, not a special few.
b: Hoi hagioi, "the holy ones," is used in Acts for the believers in Jerusalem, Lydda and Joppa (9:13, 32, 41), and Paul uses it in almost every letter for all the members of a church (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:2). It means people set apart for God, as Israel was called a holy people (Exodus 19:6). The later Christian use of "saint" for people of outstanding holiness, honored after death, grew from it, but here it means every believer.

a: kept trying to push them into blasphemy
p: The verb tense means "tried to force." Later Roman judges also tested Christians by making them curse Christ.
b: The imperfect tense of ēnankazon means "I kept trying to compel," and it does not say he succeeded. "Blasphemy" here probably means speaking against Jesus, perhaps cursing his name, which to the believers was speaking against God. About fifty years later the Roman governor Pliny reported to Trajan that he let accused Christians go if they cursed Christ, "none of which, they say, those who are really Christians can be forced to do" (Letters 10.96). Paul himself later wrote that no one speaking by God's Spirit says "Jesus is cursed" (1 Corinthians 12:3).

a: All of us dropped to the ground
p: Acts tells Paul's call three times (9, 22, 26). The details differ. This is the fullest and most direct.
b: In chapter 9 the companions stand speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one (9:7). In chapter 22 they see the light but do not hear the voice of the one speaking (22:9). Here they all fall to the ground. In chapters 9 and 22 Ananias brings Paul his commission; here Jesus gives it directly (26:16–18), and Ananias is not mentioned at all. Only here does the voice add the proverb about the goads. Some harmonize the details; others think Luke varies the retellings for each audience, telling a Roman court only what it needs. The chapter page sets the three side by side.

a: in Hebrew
p: Probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in the land. The name "Saul" keeps its Semitic form.
b: "In the Hebrew dialect" (tē Hebraidi dialektō) can mean Hebrew or Aramaic; Greek writers did not always separate them, and most scholars think Aramaic, the spoken language, is meant. Only this account says what language Jesus used, perhaps because the audience is Greek-speaking and needs to be told. A small detail supports it: in all three accounts the voice calls him Saoul, the Hebrew form of the name, not Saulos, the Greek form Luke uses everywhere else (9:4; 22:7; 26:14). Ananias, a Jew of Damascus, uses the same form when he greets him (9:17; 22:13).
orig: τῇ Ἑβραΐδι διαλέκτῳ (tē Hebraidi dialektō); Σαοὺλ Σαούλ (Saoul, Saoul)

a: Kicking against the goads is hard on you
p: A Greek proverb from the ox field, used by Euripides of a man who fought a god. A real echo, or just a proverb?
b: A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen; an ox that kicked back only hurt itself. The saying was a common Greek proverb: Pindar has it (Pythian 2.94–95), and Aeschylus (Agamemnon 1624). In Euripides' Bacchae, the god Dionysus warns King Pentheus, who is persecuting the god's followers and imprisoning them, that he should not "kick against the goads," a man fighting a god (lines 794–795). Some scholars think Luke meant his educated readers to catch that parallel; others think the proverb was simply common. Either way the point is the same: resisting God's call is painful and useless. Gamaliel had warned of "fighting against God" (5:39). The KJV also has the saying at 9:5 (see there).

a: stand up on your feet
p: Jesus commissions Paul in the words of Ezekiel's, Jeremiah's and Isaiah's calls. Paul did the same in his letters.
b: "Stand up on your feet" is how God addresses Ezekiel when he calls him (Ezekiel 2:1). "I will keep taking you out of danger" and "I am sending you" (26:17) recall God's promise to young Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:7–8), and "to open their eyes... from darkness to light" (26:18) recalls the servant of the LORD (Isaiah 42:7, 16). Paul describes his own call the same way in Galatians 1:15, echoing Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1. Krister Stendahl argued from passages like these that Paul experienced a prophetic call more than a conversion: he did not change religions, he received a mission. Others answer that the change was so deep that "conversion" fits too.
r: 26:17–18; Ezekiel 2:1; Jeremiah 1:5; Jeremiah 1:7–8; Isaiah 42:7; Isaiah 49:1; Galatians 1:15–16

a: my helper and my witness
p: Hypēretēs is an assistant, the word Luke used for "servants of the word." Witness is Acts' key word.
b: Hypēretēs is an attendant or assistant, someone who carries out another's orders. Luke's Gospel opens with eyewitnesses who became "servants of the word" (Luke 1:2), the same noun. "Witness" (martys) is the calling Jesus gave the apostles in 1:8, and Ananias gave Paul in 22:15. Paul will be a witness both to what he has seen and to what Jesus will yet show him: further visions follow in 18:9, 22:17–21, 23:11 and 27:23. The Greek "seen me" is in the critical text but not in the Byzantine text (see the variant).

a: from darkness to light
p: Paul's mission is Isaiah's servant's mission. The man who was blinded on the road is sent to open eyes.
b: Isaiah's servant was to be "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6), sent "to open blind eyes" (Isaiah 42:7), and God promised, "Ahead of them I will make the darkness light" (Isaiah 42:16). Jesus read the Greek of Isaiah 61:1, with its "recovering of sight to the blind," at Nazareth (Luke 4:18). The same cluster of words returns in Colossians 1:12–14: the inheritance of the holy ones in the light, rescue from the authority of darkness, and forgiveness of sins. This account does not mention that Paul himself was blinded (9:8–9; 22:11); the reader who knows chapter 9 hears the irony.
r: 9:8–9; 13:47; Isaiah 42:6–7; Isaiah 42:16; Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18; Colossians 1:12–14; 1 Peter 2:9

a: made holy by faith in me
p: The phrase can go with "made holy" or with "receive." Either way, faith in Jesus is the way in.
b: The Greek ends "among those made holy, by faith, the faith in me." The phrase can attach to "made holy" (people are sanctified by trusting Jesus) or to the whole sentence (they receive forgiveness and inheritance by faith). The meaning hardly changes. The perfect participle hēgiasmenois, "who have been made holy," is the same word Paul used in his farewell at Miletus about "the inheritance among all who have been made holy" (20:32). "Inheritance" (klēros) is literally a "lot": a share of land, as the tribes received in Canaan by lot, now a share in God's people.
orig: ἐν τοῖς ἡγιασμένοις πίστει τῇ εἰς ἐμέ (en tois hēgiasmenois pistei tē eis eme)

a: then through the whole countryside of Judea
p: Paul's letters say the churches of Judea did not know him by sight. Acts says he preached there.
b: In Galatians 1:22 Paul writes that after his call the churches of Judea "did not know me by sight." Here he says he preached "through the whole countryside of Judea." The Greek is also awkward at this point: the phrase stands in a different case from the words around it, and some scholars think it was added by an early copyist. Others think Paul is summarizing his whole career, including later visits (9:28–29; 11:29–30; 15:3–4; 21:15), or that Galatians refers only to the first years after his call. The tension is real and is noted by commentators on both sides.

a: live out works that are worthy of repentance
t: The message in Paul's own summary
p: Repent, turn to God, do works that fit repentance: John the Baptist's words. Where is grace and faith?
b: "Works worthy of repentance" echoes John the Baptist: "So produce fruit worthy of repentance" (Matthew 3:8; compare Luke 3:8). Readers of Paul's letters may miss his themes of grace, faith and the cross here. Philipp Vielhauer argued that the Paul of Acts is not the Paul of the letters, a key point in the critical case that Acts was written by someone who did not know Paul well. Others reply that Paul's letters also call for repentance and good works (Romans 2:4–10; 1 Thessalonians 1:9), that faith has just been named (26:18), and that a speech to a king differs from a letter to a church.
orig: ἄξια τῆς μετανοίας ἔργα (axia tēs metanoias erga)

a: that the Messiah was to suffer
p: Greek ei, "whether," may introduce headings of a debate. A suffering Messiah was not what most Jews expected.
b: The Greek has ei pathētos ho Christos, ei prōtos..., "whether the Messiah is one who suffers, whether he is first...": perhaps the questions Paul argued from Scripture, as a list of topics. Luke's risen Jesus taught that "the Messiah must suffer" from Moses and the Prophets (Luke 24:26, 46). Most Jews of the time expected a victorious Messiah. The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah calls the servant of Isaiah 52:13 "my servant the Messiah" but gives the suffering of chapter 53 to others, and the Talmud later speaks of a Messiah son of Joseph who would be killed (Bavli Sukkah 52a). Paul's claim needed arguing, and he argued it from the Scriptures.
orig: εἰ παθητὸς ὁ Χριστός (ei pathētos ho Christos)

a: the first one raised out of death
p: Others were raised and died again. Jesus is the first of the final resurrection, the firstfruits.
b: Elijah, Elisha, Jesus and Peter raised the dead (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4; Luke 7:11–17; Acts 9:36–42), but those people died again. Jesus is "the first" of the resurrection to the life of the age to come. Paul calls him "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20); Colossians 1:18 and Revelation call him "the firstborn of the dead" (Revelation 1:5). And the light he announces is the light of Isaiah's servant: "I will give you as a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6), the verse Paul quoted at Pisidian Antioch (13:47) and Simeon sang over the baby Jesus (Luke 2:32).
orig: πρῶτος ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν (prōtos ex anastaseōs nekrōn)

a: All those books of yours
p: Ta grammata, "letters," means study, books. Festus hears resurrection talk as the raving of a bookish man.
b: Ta polla grammata, "the many letters," means much reading and study; the KJV's "much learning" is the sense. Festus has heard Paul quote Moses and the Prophets and talk of a man risen from the dead, and he can only explain it as scholarly madness. Mainomai, "to rave, be mad," is the word the servants used of Rhoda (12:15) and opponents of Jesus (John 10:20). Paul knew how the message sounded to Gentiles: "foolishness" (1 Corinthians 1:23). Ironically, the Jewish leaders had once marveled that Peter and John were "unlettered" (agrammatoi, 4:13).
orig: τὰ πολλά σε γράμματα εἰς μανίαν περιτρέπει (ta polla se grammata eis manian peritrepei)

a: sound of mind
p: Paul answers with the classic Greek virtue of sober good sense, the opposite of the madness Festus charged.
b: Sōphrosynē was one of the four virtues Greek philosophers prized: self-command, soundness of mind, moderation. It is the exact opposite of mania. Paul answers the Roman in the vocabulary of the philosophers: his words are "true" and "sober." Luke's apologetic aim shows here. The Christian message, he wants his educated readers to see, is not frenzy but reasoned truth.
orig: ἀληθείας καὶ σωφροσύνης ῥήματα (alētheias kai sōphrosynēs rhēmata)

a: This thing was not done off in a corner
p: A Greek phrase used to mock philosophers who hid away. Paul says the Christian story happened in public.
b: "In a corner" was a stock Greek phrase for private, hidden talk. In Plato's Gorgias (485d) Callicles sneers that a philosopher spends his life "whispering in a corner with three or four boys" instead of speaking in public. Abraham Malherbe showed that Paul uses the language of public philosophical debate here. The events of the faith were open: a public execution at Passover, an empty tomb in Jerusalem, preaching in the temple courts, a movement known across the empire. Agrippa, who governed Jewish affairs, must have heard of them.

a: With so little
p: The KJV's "almost" misreads en oligō, "in a short time" or "with little effort." Agrippa is probably sarcastic.
b: The KJV made this one of the best-known lines in the Bible: "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian," and from it came Philip P. Bliss's gospel hymn "Almost Persuaded" (1871). But en oligō does not mean "almost" (Greek would say par' oligon or oligou dein). It means "in a little," either "in a short time" or "with little effort." Most scholars hear a dry, ironic king: "Do you think so quickly to make a Christian of me?" Paul's reply picks up the phrase: "Little or much" (26:29). Agrippa may also be trapped. If he says he believes the prophets, Paul will press him; if he says no, he offends the Jews who honor them.

a: a Christian
p: Christianos appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the mouths of outsiders or accusers.
b: Christianos uses a Latin ending, -ianus, "belonging to the party of," like Herodianus, "Herodian." It first appears at Antioch (11:26), here on the lips of a king, and in 1 Peter 4:16, where someone suffers "as a Christian" before a court. The Roman historian Tacitus says the crowd called them Chrestiani when Nero blamed them for the fire of Rome in AD 64 (Annals 15.44). The believers' own names in Acts were the disciples, the brothers, the saints and the Way. Agrippa uses the label outsiders used.

a: apart from these chains
p: A courteous, even witty ending: Paul wishes the king everything he has, except the handcuffs.
b: Desmoi are bonds or chains. Paul may have been chained to a soldier even in this hearing (28:20). His closing line is gracious and a little playful: he wishes all his hearers, kings included, the faith he has, but not the chains it has cost him. John Chrysostom admired it as a model of a prisoner's freedom of spirit. The Greek "little or much" (en oligō kai en megalō) answers Agrippa's "with so little" and may mean "whether quickly or slowly" or "whether by small or great means."
orig: παρεκτὸς τῶν δεσμῶν τούτων (parektos tōn desmōn toutōn)

a: if only he had not appealed to Caesar
t: Too late to set him free?
p: In law, Festus might still have released Paul. In politics, no governor would undo an appeal to the emperor.
b: Could Festus have released Paul after the appeal? A. N. Sherwin-White argued that the law did not strictly forbid it, but that no governor would cut across the emperor's right to hear a case that had been sent to him, least of all for a prisoner the Temple leaders wanted dead. Agrippa's remark is less legal than human: the man is innocent, and his own move has bound him. Luke's readers know the larger answer. The Lord had said Paul must bear witness in Rome (23:11), and the appeal is how he gets there.

a: Once our sailing for Italy was settled
p: The narrator says "we" for the last and longest time. An eyewitness, a convention of sea stories, or a source?
b: The "we" passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) end here with the longest one. The traditional view, held since Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.14.1), is that the author, Luke, was with Paul. Vernon Robbins argued that ancient sea-voyage stories were told in the first person as a literary convention; critics answered that many ancient voyage stories are in the third person, and that the "we" here begins and ends with no regard to sea travel. Martin Dibelius thought Luke used a travel diary; Richard Pervo, that the "we" is a device to make fiction vivid. The detail of this chapter, its sailing terms, its courses and timings, is the strongest argument of those who see an eyewitness.

a: a centurion of the Emperor's Cohort
p: A cohort called Sebastē, "Augustan." Its identity is debated. Julius is one of several decent centurions in Luke.
b: "The Emperor's Cohort" is speira Sebastē, the "Augustan" cohort. Inscriptions mention a cohors Augusta in the region of Syria in the first century. Others link it with the "Sebastenes," troops recruited from Sebaste (Samaria) and stationed at Caesarea (Josephus, Antiquities 19.365; 20.122). Ramsay thought Julius was one of the officers who carried messages and escorted prisoners between the provinces and Rome. Whatever his unit, Julius behaves well: he lets Paul visit friends (27:3) and later saves his life (27:43). Luke's centurions are often admirable (Luke 7:2–10; Acts 10; 22:26).

a: Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica
p: A companion since Ephesus. Paul later calls him "my fellow prisoner."
b: Aristarchus was dragged into the theater at Ephesus with Gaius (19:29) and traveled with Paul to Jerusalem with the collection (20:4). He sails with Paul now, perhaps as his attendant, perhaps going home to Macedonia. Paul's letters name him as "my fellow prisoner" (Colossians 4:10) and a co-worker (Philemon 24). The ship from Adramyttium, a port near Troas, was a coastal trader working its way home. The centurion's plan was to find a larger ship to Italy along the way, which he did at Myra (27:6).

a: his friends
p: With the article, "the friends" may be a name believers used for one another, as in 3 John 14.
b: The Greek has "the friends," with the article, and some scholars think it was one of the early names Christians used for themselves, as it was among some philosophical schools. 3 John 14 ends, "The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name." Jesus called his disciples "friends" (John 15:14–15; Luke 12:4). Believers had lived in Phoenicia since the scattering after Stephen's death (11:19; 15:3; 21:3–7). For a prisoner, friends who brought food and care made a long voyage survivable.

a: we kept to the sheltered side of Cyprus
p: In the eastern Mediterranean the summer winds blow from the west and northwest. Ships bound west hugged the coasts.
b: Through the summer, steady winds blow from the northwest across the eastern Mediterranean. A ship heading west from Sidon could not sail straight across, so it passed east and north of Cyprus, using the island for shelter and the coastal breezes and westward current along Cilicia and Pamphylia. James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman who studied this voyage in the 1840s, showed that every course Luke gives fits the winds of the season. Alexandrian grain ships bound for Rome often took the same northern route, which is why one was waiting at Myra (27:6).

a: a ship out of Alexandria bound for Italy
p: Egypt fed Rome. Big grain ships sailed for Italy, and the emperor rewarded owners who took the risk late in the year.
b: Rome depended on grain shipped from Egypt; Josephus' Agrippa says Egypt fed the city for four months of the year (Jewish War 2.386). The ships were big: this one carried 276 people (27:37) and a cargo of wheat (27:38). Lucian's dialogue The Ship describes an Alexandrian grain carrier, the Isis, blown off course by way of Sidon and the Lycian coast. Claudius had promised to cover shipowners' losses from storms, to keep grain coming even in the risky season (Suetonius, Claudius 18–19), which may explain why the owner pressed on so late (27:11).

a: a spot known as Fair Havens
p: The bay on Crete's south coast still bears the name, Kaloi Limenes. Its anchorage is open to winter gales.
b: Kaloi Limenes, "Fair Havens," is still the name of a small bay on the south coast of Crete, just east of the headland where the coast turns north and the shelter from the northwest wind ends. Ruins near it have been identified with Lasea. The bay is open to the east and south, which is why the sailors thought it a poor place to spend the winter (27:12). Luke's place names here are precise, though no other ancient writer mentions Fair Havens by this name.

a: the Fast was already past
p: Luke dates the voyage by the Jewish calendar. After the Day of Atonement, the sailing season was closing.
b: "The Fast" is the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, on the tenth day of the seventh month, when Israel was told, "you are to humble yourselves" (Leviticus 16:29). It falls in September or October. The Roman writer Vegetius (about 400) says sailing was safe until mid-September, doubtful until 11 November, and closed from then until 10 March (Epitome 4.39). Luke, writing for Gentiles, still tells time by Israel's holy days, as Paul did (20:6, 16). Since the date of Yom Kippur moves, some have tried to date the voyage by it; Ramsay argued that in AD 59 it fell late, in early October, which would fit the story.

a: Our own lives are at stake too
p: Paul predicts loss of life, but no one dies (27:22, 44). Was he giving advice, or did God change the outcome?
b: Paul says "I can tell" (theōrō, "I see, I perceive"), not "the Spirit says." Many readers take this as the advice of a seasoned traveler: Paul had been shipwrecked three times already (2 Corinthians 11:25). Later God promises that no life will be lost (27:22–24). Some see a prophecy that was fulfilled in part, with the ship and cargo lost; others see a warning that God then overruled in mercy, as with Jonah's Nineveh. Luke shows a Paul who is right about the sea, and whose word saves everyone.

a: the helmsman and the shipowner
p: The pilot and the owner (or captain) gave advice. Why did a centurion decide what a merchant ship did?
b: The kybernētēs was the helmsman or sailing master; the nauklēros was the shipowner or the man who chartered the ship. That a centurion seems to decide is surprising. Some think the grain ships worked under state contract and the senior officer on board had the last word; others think Luke simply means the centurion, as the most important passenger, accepted the experts' plan; still others think "the majority" in 27:12 means a council of the ship's officers. Either way, Luke sets the professionals' confidence beside Paul's warning, and the sea proves Paul right.
orig: τῷ κυβερνήτῃ καὶ τῷ ναυκλήρῳ (tō kybernētē kai tō nauklērō)

a: Phoenix is a Cretan harbor
p: A harbor farther west on Crete, usually placed at Loutro or near Phineka. Its "facing" is debated.
b: Phoenix lay about forty miles west along the Cretan coast. It is usually placed at modern Loutro, the one good harbor on that coast, or at the nearby bay of Phineka, which keeps the ancient name. The Greek says it "looks toward Lips and toward Chorus," the southwest and northwest winds. Loutro actually opens to the east. Smith argued that the phrase means looking "down" those winds, the direction they blow toward, which fits Loutro; others prefer Phineka and the plain sense. The disagreement shows how closely scholars have checked the details of this chapter.
orig: βλέποντα κατὰ λίβα καὶ κατὰ χῶρον (bleponta kata liba kai kata chōron)

a: a typhoon-like wind
p: Typhōnikos, "like Typhon," the storm monster of Greek myth. Sailors still fear the winter northeaster.
b: Typhōnikos means a whirling, violent wind, named for Typhon, the monster of storms in Greek myth; English "typhoon" comes partly from the same word. It came "rushing down" off the mountains of Crete, which rise to over 7,000 feet. The northeaster that strikes the central Mediterranean in winter is still feared; in Malta it is called the gregale. Luke gives its sailors' name, Eurakylōn (see the variant).

a: could not look the wind in the eye
t: Eye to eye with the wind
p: Antophthalmein means "to look in the eye." Ancient ships had eyes painted on their bows.
b: Antophthalmein means "to face, to look someone in the eye." Ancient ships often had eyes painted or carved on each side of the bow, so a sailor could speak of a ship looking into the wind. Unable to point its head into the storm, the ship turned and ran before it. The Plain keeps the picture because Luke's Greek does.

a: the skiff
p: Merchant ships towed a small boat astern. In a storm it filled with water and had to be hauled aboard.
b: The skaphē was the ship's small boat, normally towed behind. In a gale it fills and can smash against the stern, so the crew hauled it on board in the shelter of Cauda, with great effort; Luke's "we" suggests the passengers helped. The skiff comes back in the story: the sailors try to escape in it (27:30), and the soldiers cut it loose (27:32).

a: used cables as braces, lashing them around the hull
p: Cables were passed around the hull to hold the planks together. Exactly how is still debated.
b: Boētheiai are "helps," here the cables or tackle used to hypozōnnynai, "undergird," the ship. Greek naval records list hypozōmata, girding cables, as standard gear for warships. Scholars disagree on how they were used: passed under the hull crosswise and tightened ("frapping," as sailors did into the 1800s), run lengthwise from bow to stern, or stretched inside the hull. The purpose is clear: to keep the planks from working loose as the ship strained.
orig: βοηθείαις ἐχρῶντο ὑποζωννύντες τὸ πλοῖον (boētheiais echrōnto hypozōnnyntes to ploion)

a: the shoals of Syrtis
p: The shallow gulfs off Libya, the sailors' nightmare, with shifting sandbanks far from land.
b: The Syrtis (Greater Syrtis, the Gulf of Sidra off Libya) was notorious for shallow, shifting sandbanks where ships stuck far from shore. Strabo describes the danger, and Josephus' Agrippa calls the Syrtes terrible even to hear of (Jewish War 2.381). A northeaster blowing from Crete would drive a ship straight toward them, which is why the crew did all they could to slow the drift.

a: they let down the gear
p: The Greek just says "the gear." A sea anchor dragged behind, or the mainsail and yard taken down?
b: To skeuos is "the equipment, the gear" and the phrase does not say which. Some translations say "sea anchor": a drag let out behind to slow the drift. Others think the crew lowered the great mainsail and its yard, leaving a small storm sail to hold the ship on a course away from the Syrtis. Smith argued for the second and calculated that a ship lying to on the starboard tack, drifting west by north about a mile and a half an hour, would cover the distance from Cauda to Malta in about the thirteen or fourteen days Luke gives (27:27).

a: heaving the cargo into the sea
p: A storm, sailors throwing cargo overboard, a servant of God on board: Jonah's story is close by.
b: When the great storm struck Jonah's ship, the sailors threw the cargo into the sea to lighten it (Jonah 1:5). Readers since the early church have noticed the parallels: a storm, a ship of Gentile sailors, cargo thrown out, a servant of God aboard who confesses the God he serves (Jonah 1:9; Acts 27:23), and in the end all are saved. The difference is sharp: Jonah was running from his mission to the Gentiles, and the storm stopped when he was thrown out; Paul is on his way to his mission, and everyone is saved because he stays. See the chapter's theory box.

a: every hope that we would be saved
p: Luke uses the vocabulary of salvation for the rescue at sea seven times. Readers would hear both senses.
b: The word families of sōzō, "save," and sōtēria, "rescue, salvation," run through the story: no hope of being saved (27:20), "there is no way for you to be saved" (27:31), "this is for your rescue" (27:34), the centurion wanting to bring Paul safely through (27:43), all brought safely through (27:44; 28:1), the islanders' "He came safely through the sea" (28:4). The Plain renders diasōzō "bring safely through" each time so the chain stays visible. Luke's readers knew these as the words of their own salvation; the voyage reads like a parable of it, though Luke never says so.
orig: ἐλπὶς πᾶσα τοῦ σῴζεσθαι ἡμᾶς (elpis pasa tou sōzesthai hēmas)

a: Then you would not have gained this harm and this loss
p: Kerdainō means "gain," but with a loss as its object it can mean "spare oneself." The sense is the same.
b: The Greek verb kerdēsai normally means "to gain, to profit." With an object like "harm" or "loss," Greek could use it to mean "to avoid, to be spared" a loss, as if escaping a loss were a gain. So the clause can be read "you should have... spared yourselves this harm," or as dry irony, "and gained this harm." Either way Paul is saying "I told you so," not to gloat but to win a hearing for what he says next.
orig: κερδῆσαί τε τὴν ὕβριν ταύτην καὶ τὴν ζημίαν (kerdēsai te tēn hybrin tautēn kai tēn zēmian)

a: an angel of the God who owns me, the God I worship
p: Paul names his God to pagan sailors as a servant names his master. Jonah did the same.
b: "Whose I am and whom I worship" is how Paul introduces his God to a ship of people who worship many gods. It sounds like Jonah's confession to his shipmates: "The LORD is the one I fear, the God of the heavens" (Jonah 1:9). Paul has had night visions before at turning points (16:9; 18:9–10; 23:11). This one confirms the promise of 23:11 that he would bear witness in Rome. For Luke's readers it means that no storm, shipwreck or court could stop God's plan.
orig: τοῦ θεοῦ, οὗ εἰμι, ᾧ καὶ λατρεύω (tou theou, hou eimi, hō kai latreuō)

a: God has made you a gift of everyone who is sailing with you
p: The angel speaks as if Paul had prayed for his shipmates. Some see Abraham's prayer for Sodom here.
b: "Has made you a gift" (kecharistai) implies that the 275 others are saved for Paul's sake, perhaps in answer to his prayers. Readers have compared Abraham pleading for the city for the sake of the righteous in it (Genesis 18:23–32) and Lot's family saved for Abraham's sake (Genesis 19:29). Others stress simply that Paul must reach Rome, and God's protection of him covers everyone on board. Luke uses the same verb in 25:11 (see the note there).
orig: κεχάρισταί σοι ὁ θεὸς πάντας (kecharistai soi ho theos pantas)

a: drifting back and forth across the Adria
p: In ancient usage, the open sea between Greece, Italy, Sicily and Africa, not only today's Adriatic.
b: Ancient geographers used "the Adria" for the whole central Mediterranean south of the Adriatic gulf, the open water between Crete, Greece, Sicily and Malta. Josephus says he too was shipwrecked "in the middle of the Adria" on his way to Rome a few years later, about AD 63; of some 600 aboard, about 80 survived by swimming all night until a ship from Cyrene picked them up (Life 15). Fourteen days fits the drift James Smith calculated from Cauda to Malta (see 27:17). Some who place the wreck elsewhere argue from this word (see the note at 28:1).

a: measured twenty fathoms
p: A fathom is about six feet: 120 feet, then 90. The depths match the approach to St Paul's Bay in Malta.
b: A fathom (orguia) was the span of a man's outstretched arms, about six feet, so the readings were about 120 and 90 feet. The sailors had heard breakers in the dark. James Smith checked the British Admiralty charts of the approach to St Paul's Bay on the northeast coast of Malta and found that a ship drifting in past the point of Koura would pass over twenty and then fifteen fathoms just as Luke says, with breakers audible on the point. Those who place the wreck elsewhere answer that many coasts have such depths.

a: four anchors from the stern
p: Anchors from the back kept the ship pointed toward shore, ready to run in at daylight.
b: Ships usually anchored from the bow. Anchoring from the stern kept the ship from swinging around in the wind and left it pointed at the shore, ready to be run aground when day came (27:39–40). Four anchors show how hard the wind was blowing. "Kept praying" (ēuchonto) can also mean "kept wishing"; on this ship both would be true.
orig: ἐκ πρύμνης ῥίψαντες ἀγκύρας τέσσαρας (ek prymnēs rhipsantes ankyras tessaras)

a: Meanwhile the sailors were looking for a way to get off the ship
p: Paul believed the crew meant to escape. Some think they were truly laying anchors, and cutting the skiff cost the ship dearly.
b: Luke reports the sailors' plan as an escape attempt, and Paul's warning to the soldiers as wise: without the crew, no one could handle the ship at dawn. Some commentators wonder whether the sailors were really setting bow anchors, as they said, and whether cutting away the skiff was a costly overreaction, since the boat could have ferried people ashore. Luke tells it as Paul read it. In Luke's telling, the prisoner has become the one whose word the soldiers obey.

a: Not a hair will be lost from the head of one of you
p: An old Israelite oath of safety, and a promise Jesus gave his followers.
b: "Not a hair" was an old way of promising complete safety. The people swore of Jonathan, "not a single hair from his head will drop to the ground" (1 Samuel 14:45), and David promised the woman of Tekoa the same for her son (2 Samuel 14:11). Jesus told his disciples that even in persecution "not one hair from your head will be lost" (Luke 21:18). Paul applies the promise to a shipload of sailors, soldiers and prisoners who mostly did not share his faith.
r: 1 Samuel 14:45; 2 Samuel 14:11; 1 Kings 1:52; Matthew 10:30; Luke 12:7; Luke 21:18

a: he took a loaf, thanked God before everyone, broke it
p: The words are the words of the Last Supper. Was this a Eucharist, an ordinary Jewish grace, or a sign of both?
b: Luke uses the same verbs as at the Last Supper (Luke 22:19) and Emmaus (Luke 24:30): took bread, gave thanks, broke it. Many on board were pagans, so most commentators think this was an ordinary meal, opened as every Jewish meal was with thanks to God, and not a Eucharist. Others think Luke means readers to hear the church's meal in it: the breaking of bread (2:42; 20:7, 11) offered as a sign of salvation to all. Some later manuscripts (614 and others, reported by Metzger) add "giving also to us," which makes it look more like a shared Christian meal among the "we."
orig: λαβὼν ἄρτον εὐχαρίστησεν τῷ θεῷ... καὶ κλάσας (labōn arton eucharistēsen tō theō... kai klasas)

a: the steering oars
p: Ancient ships steered with two large paddle-rudders, one on each side of the stern.
b: Ships of this period had no hinged rudder on the stern post. They were steered by two large oars, pēdalia, one on each quarter of the stern. While the ship lay at anchor the oars were lashed up out of the water; now the crew freed them to steer for the beach. The "small sail at the front" (artemōn) was a foresail on a forward-leaning mast, used for steering more than speed. Every move in these verses matches what a crew would do to run a ship onto a beach.
orig: τὰς ζευκτηρίας τῶν πηδαλίων (tas zeuktērias tōn pēdaliōn)

a: a place where two seas meet
p: Dithalassos may mean a sandbar, a reef, or a channel between an island and the shore.
b: Topos dithalassos, "a place with sea on two sides," is rare. It may mean a sandbank or reef with deep water on both sides, a spit, or a narrow channel where two currents meet. At St Paul's Bay, Smith pointed to the narrow channel between the small St Paul's Islands and the Maltese shore, where a ship would strike a bottom of mud and clay that grips the bow while the stern is beaten by the surf. The KJV's "where two seas met" is the literal sense.

a: The soldiers made up their minds to kill the prisoners
p: A guard who lost his prisoner could pay with his life. The soldiers' plan was brutal but logical.
b: Roman guards were answerable for their prisoners. Herod Agrippa I executed the guards after Peter escaped (12:19), and the jailer at Philippi was ready to kill himself (16:27). Killing the prisoners would prevent escapes the soldiers would be blamed for. The centurion stops it "wanting to bring Paul safely through": Paul's presence again saves the others, as 27:24 promised. In Luke's telling, one prisoner's life is the reason the rest are spared.

a: Malta
p: Most scholars accept Malta and St Paul's Bay. Others have argued for Mljet in the Adriatic or for Kefalonia.
b: Luke calls the island Melitē, the ancient name of Malta, and Malta's tradition goes back many centuries. James Smith's study of the winds, drift and soundings (see 27:17, 27:28) convinced most scholars that the wreck happened at St Paul's Bay on Malta's northeast coast. Two other views have been argued. A tradition at least as old as the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII (900s; On the Administration of the Empire 36) placed it on Mljet, an island off Croatia also once called Melite, because the Greek speaks of "the Adria" (27:27); but a northeaster could not drive a ship there from Crete. In 1987 Heinz Warnecke argued for Kefalonia off western Greece; most scholars have rejected that too, since Kefalonia was never called Melite and the route does not fit the winds.

a: The local people
p: Barbaroi meant people who did not speak Greek, not savages. The Maltese spoke a form of Punic.
b: Luke calls the islanders barbaroi (28:2, 4). The word imitated the sound of foreign speech ("bar-bar") and meant anyone whose language was not Greek; Paul uses it that way too (Romans 1:14; 1 Corinthians 14:11). The KJV's "the barbarous people" sounds like cruelty, but Luke means the opposite: these non-Greeks are kind "beyond the ordinary" (philanthrōpia), the very virtue Greeks prized. The common people of Malta spoke a form of Punic, the Phoenician language of Carthage, while officials used Greek and Latin.

a: A viper
p: No venomous vipers live on Malta today. Was the snake harmless, has the species died out, or is the point the miracle?
b: Echidna means a viper, a poisonous snake, and the islanders clearly expected Paul to die. But no venomous vipers live on Malta now. Some think vipers lived there when the island was more wooded and have since died out. Some think the snake was a nonpoisonous kind the islanders mistook; Luke says it "clamped onto" (kathēpsen) his hand, not that it bit. Others say Luke tells the story as a sign of God's protection and the question of species misses his point. All three views have defenders among careful scholars.

a: Justice
p: Dikē, Justice, was a goddess who hunted down murderers. A Greek poem tells of a shipwrecked man killed by a snake.
b: Dikē, "Justice," was worshiped as a goddess, the daughter of Zeus who sat by his throne and saw that wrongdoers were punished. The islanders reason as many ancient people did: a man who escaped the sea and then met a viper must be a murderer whom Justice would not let go. A short Greek poem in the Greek Anthology (7.290) tells of a sailor who survived a shipwreck, only to be killed by a viper as he lay on the Libyan shore. The verdict: the parallel is real but general. It shows the logic of retribution Luke's readers knew, which the story then overturns.

a: felt no ill at all
p: Jesus promised his messengers they could tread on snakes unharmed. A later ending of Mark says the same.
b: Jesus told the seventy-two, "I have given you the authority to walk on top of snakes and scorpions" (Luke 10:19), and Psalm 91 promises the one who trusts in God, "Lion and cobra you will walk upon" (Psalm 91:13). The longer ending of Mark, a later addition, includes among the signs "They will take up snakes" (Mark 16:18). Paul does not seek out the danger. Luke presents the escape as God's vindication after the storm: the gods of Malta's people do not condemn him, and the sea did not take him.

a: began saying he was a god
p: At Lystra Paul tore his clothes when people called him a god. Here Luke reports it without comment.
b: At Lystra the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and Paul ran in, protesting that they were only human (14:11–18). Herod Agrippa I accepted the crowd's cry that his was a god's voice, and was struck down (12:22–23). Here the islanders swing from "murderer" to "god" and Luke records no protest. Some think Paul never heard it; some think Luke abbreviates. Many see the verse as humor at the islanders' quick change of verdict, in a story that keeps showing God at work through an ordinary, shipwrecked man.

a: the first man of the island
p: Inscriptions found on Malta use the same title, "first of the Maltese," for a leading official.
b: "First man" (prōtos) sounds vague, but Greek and Latin inscriptions found on Malta use it as a title for a leading magistrate of the island, "first of the Maltese." Writers such as Ramsay and Hemer counted it among the small details that show Luke's local knowledge. Publius is a Latin first name; he may have been the island's chief Roman official or a local notable. His hospitality fits the kindness the islanders had already shown.
orig: τῷ πρώτῳ τῆς νήσου (tō prōtō tēs nēsou)

a: bouts of fever and dysentery
p: Precise medical terms, once used to argue that Luke was a doctor. The argument has been both pressed and doubted.
b: Luke writes "fevers" in the plural, recurring bouts, and dysenterion, "dysentery." William Hobart (1882) gathered such terms to show that the author wrote like a trained physician, as Colossians 4:14 calls Luke. Henry Cadbury replied that Greek writers with no medical training used the same words, so the language proves no profession. Some have guessed the illness was "Malta fever" (brucellosis), caught from goats' milk and described on the island in the 1800s; that is only a guess. Jesus healed Peter's mother-in-law of a fever (Luke 4:38–39).

a: put his hands on him, and healed him
t: Prayer and the laying on of hands
p: Paul prays first, then lays on hands. Jesus healed this way, and so did Ananias for Paul himself.
b: Jesus healed by laying his hands on the sick (Luke 4:40; 13:13). Ananias laid hands on the blinded Saul (9:12, 17). Paul now does the same, after prayer, which makes clear that the power is God's. The scene echoes Jesus healing a fever in a leading man's household (Luke 4:38–39) and the crowds who followed (Luke 4:40), as Luke's Gospel and Acts mirror each other again. How Christians today understand such healings is the subject of the card on this chapter.

a: they were cured
p: Therapeuō can mean "heal" or "treat." Some think Luke the doctor treated the sick, which is why they honored "us."
b: In 28:8 Paul "healed" (iasato) Publius' father. In 28:9 the others "were cured" (etherapeuonto), a verb that can mean medical treatment as well as healing. Because the islanders then honored "us" (28:10), some scholars have suggested that Luke the physician treated the sick while Paul prayed. Most think the two verbs are used here as near synonyms, as they often are in the Gospels. "Honors" (timai) can also mean gifts or payment, as in English "honorarium."

a: Three months later
p: The seas reopened in early spring. A ship that had wintered at Malta left as soon as it could.
b: The wreck happened in late autumn, so three months on Malta brings the story to about February. Pliny the Elder says the west wind of spring opened the seas to sailors about 8 February (Natural History 2.122), earlier than the March date Vegetius gives for normal sailing. Another Alexandrian grain ship had wintered in Malta's harbor, and its owner would want to reach Italy early, when grain fetched its best price.

a: the Twins, the sons of Zeus
p: Castor and Pollux, the sons of Zeus, were the sailors' gods. After the true God's rescue, Luke notes the ship's pagan emblem.
b: Dioskouroi means "sons of Zeus": the twins Castor and Pollux, whom sailors called on in storms and saw in the lights that play on masts. Horace prays for a friend's ship to "the brothers of Helen, shining stars" (Odes 1.3.2). Ships were named for the image carved or painted on the bow, so this ship was in effect the Twins. Luke reports it plainly. Many readers hear a quiet contrast: the travelers have just been saved by the God Paul serves, and now they sail under the protection of gods who had not saved anyone. The verdict: the cult is real and well attested; the irony is Luke's, if it is there at all.

a: Puteoli
p: Italy's great port for the Alexandrian grain fleet, on the Bay of Naples, with a Jewish community and believers.
b: Puteoli (modern Pozzuoli) on the Bay of Naples was the chief port where the Alexandrian grain ships unloaded before the harbor at Ostia was finished. Seneca describes crowds on the docks of Puteoli watching for the Alexandrian mail ships, which could be recognized by their topsails (Letters 77.1). Josephus mentions Jews living there in Herod's time (Antiquities 17.328). That Paul found "brothers" there (28:14) shows the faith had reached Italy before any apostle; Paul had written to the Romans some three years before.

a: And that is how we came to Rome
p: Luke says "we came to Rome" here and again in 28:16. A summary first, then the story?
b: Luke announces the arrival before telling it (28:16). Some read 28:14 as a heading for what follows. Others think "Rome" here means the Roman district or road, or that Luke writes with a sense of triumph: this is the goal set at 19:21 ("I must see Rome as well") and promised in 23:11. Acts 1:8 had sent the witnesses "to the end of the earth." Whether Luke meant Rome as that end is debated (see the chapter page), but the long road from Jerusalem ends here.

a: to meet us
p: Apantēsis is the word for a city's delegation going out to escort an honored visitor. Paul uses it of meeting the Lord.
b: When an emperor or governor approached a city, its leading people went out along the road to meet him and escort him in; the Greek word for this was apantēsis. The believers of Rome walked out 33 and 43 miles to do this for a prisoner in chains. Paul used the same word for believers who will go out "to meet the Lord in the air" at his coming (1 Thessalonians 4:17), and Matthew for the bridesmaids going out to meet the bridegroom (Matthew 25:6). This is the welcome Paul receives on the Appian Way.

a: Appius' Market and at Three Taverns
p: Two stopping places on the road into Rome, about 43 and 33 Roman miles from the city.
b: Paul walked the Appian Way, the oldest of Rome's great roads. Forum Appii, "Appius' Market," was a market town about 43 Roman miles from Rome, at the end of a canal through the marshes; Horace remembered it as "stuffed with boatmen and stingy innkeepers" (Satires 1.5.3–4).
