Tres Tabernae, "Three Shops" (or Taverns), about ten miles nearer the city, is mentioned by Cicero (Letters to Atticus 2.12). Two groups of believers had come out to meet him. Paul had written that he longed to see them (Romans 1:11); now they came to see him.

a: along with the soldier assigned to guard him
p: Paul lived in his own lodging, chained to a soldier who was changed in shifts. He could receive anyone.
b: This was the lightest form of Roman military custody. Paul was chained by the wrist to a soldier (28:20), but he lived in quarters he rented himself (28:30) and could receive visitors freely. Guards were changed regularly, so over two years many soldiers of the Praetorian Guard would have heard him: if Philippians was written from Rome, that may be what Paul means when he says his chains became known "throughout the whole praetorium" (Philippians 1:13). The Byzantine text adds that the centurion handed the prisoners over to the camp commander (see the variant).

a: the men who led the Jews there
p: Rome had a large Jewish community with many synagogues, some of them named on catacomb inscriptions.
b: By Paul's day Rome had tens of thousands of Jews, many of them descendants of captives and freed slaves who lived across the Tiber (Philo, Embassy to Gaius 155). They met in many separate synagogues; inscriptions from the Jewish catacombs name more than ten, among them synagogues of the Hebrews, of the Augustesians and of the Agrippesians. There was no single chief rabbi, so Paul invited the leaders of several congregations. Claudius had expelled some Jews from Rome about AD 49 over disturbances (see 18:2), and many had returned since his death in 54.

a: from Jerusalem I was handed over, a prisoner, into Roman hands
p: Paul's words echo Jesus' predictions that he would be handed over to the Gentiles. Agabus said the same of Paul.
b: Jesus foretold that the Son of Man would be handed over into human hands and to the Gentiles (Luke 9:44; Luke 18:32), and Agabus said the Jews in Jerusalem would hand Paul over to the Gentiles (21:11). Paul's account compresses what happened: in fact Roman soldiers took him from a mob in the temple (21:30–33). Luke lets the wording mirror Jesus' passion, as so much of Paul's last journey does. To the Jews of Rome, Paul stresses that he comes not as an accuser of his people but as a Jew wronged by the process.

a: on account of Israel's hope
p: Paul's last word in his defense: he wears a chain not for a new religion but for Israel's own hope.
b: Through every hearing Paul has said the same thing: he is on trial for "the hope" (23:6; 24:15; 26:6–7). Here he calls it simply "Israel's hope": the hope that God will keep his promises to the fathers, raise the dead, and send his Messiah. Paul presents faith in Jesus as that hope fulfilled, not as a departure from it. Jewish readers of Acts such as Daniel Boyarin and Paula Fredriksen have stressed how Jewish this Paul is. The chain (halysis) is the one that tied him to his guard; Ephesians 6:20 calls him "an ambassador in a chain."
orig: ἕνεκεν τῆς ἐλπίδος τοῦ Ἰσραήλ (heneken tēs elpidos tou Israēl)

a: No letters about you have reached us from Judea
p: After two years of plots, why had no one written to Rome? Several explanations have been offered.
b: The Roman Jewish leaders say they have had no letters and no bad report. Some find this surprising after the Jerusalem leaders' long campaign. Explanations offered: Paul's ship was among the first of the season, so no letters could have arrived; the Jerusalem leaders saw little chance of winning before Caesar and let the case drop; or the Roman leaders were being cautious, not wanting to take sides in a case before the emperor. Luke may also want to show that Rome's Jews were open to hearing Paul for themselves.

a: it is spoken against everywhere
p: The same verb Simeon used of the baby Jesus: "a sign people speak against."
b: Antilegetai, "is spoken against," recalls Simeon's words over the infant Jesus in the temple: he is set for the falling and rising of many in Israel, "a sign people speak against" (Luke 2:34). Luke-Acts opens and closes on the same note. Roman writers bear out the report: Tacitus calls the Christians a group "hated for their vile deeds" (Annals 15.44), and 1 Peter tells believers that people speak against them as wrongdoers (1 Peter 2:12).

a: He bore solemn witness to the kingdom of God
t: The kingdom of God, from start to end
p: Acts begins with Jesus teaching about the kingdom of God (1:3) and ends with Paul doing the same.
b: The risen Jesus spent forty days speaking of the kingdom of God (1:3), and the book closes with Paul proclaiming it (28:31). Between them Philip (8:12) and Paul (14:22; 19:8; 20:25) preached it. Paul argues "from the law of Moses and the Prophets," as the risen Jesus did on the road to Emmaus and in Jerusalem (Luke 24:27, 44). The scene, a whole day of teaching from Scripture in a Jewish setting, is how Paul began in almost every city (13:5, 14; 17:2–3).

a: Some were persuaded by his words
p: Not all Rome's Jews refused. Some were persuaded. How much that matters for the ending is a key question.
b: "Some were persuaded" uses the same verb Luke uses for converts elsewhere (17:4). The leaders leave "at odds with one another," divided, not united against Paul. Jacob Jervell argued that this is Luke's constant picture: Israel is not rejected as a whole but divided, and the believing part of Israel is the restored people into which Gentiles are gathered (15:16–17). Others, such as Jack T. Sanders and Ernst Haenchen, read the closing words as Luke's verdict that the Jews as a people had refused. See the chapter page.

a: The Holy Spirit put it well
p: Luke says the Holy Spirit spoke through Isaiah, as he spoke through David (1:16; 4:25).
b: Acts introduces Scripture as the Spirit's speech: the Holy Spirit spoke through David's mouth (1:16; 4:25). Hebrews does the same (Hebrews 3:7; 10:15). "Put it well" (kalōs) can be bitter, as when Jesus told his critics that Isaiah had prophesied well about them (Mark 7:6; Matthew 15:7). Paul says "your fathers," not "our fathers" as at 28:17; the Byzantine text has "our" (see the variant).
orig: καλῶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐλάλησεν (kalōs to pneuma to hagion elalēsen)

a: Go to this people and say
p: Every Gospel uses Isaiah 6:9–10. Luke shortened it in his Gospel and saved the full quotation for the last scene of Acts.
b: God's commission to Isaiah is quoted in all four Gospels to explain why many did not believe Jesus (Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; John 12:40). Luke's Gospel gives only a few words of it (Luke 8:10) and holds the full text back for this moment. The Greek follows the Septuagint, word for word as in Matthew 13:14–15, and the Plain follows Matthew's wording. The Hebrew is harsher. There God tells the prophet to cause the hardness: "Make this people's heart fat" (Isaiah 6:10). In the Greek the people have done it themselves: their heart "has become sluggish." The prophecy describes a people's refusal more than God's decree.
r: Isaiah 6:9–10; Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; Luke 8:10; John 12:39–40; Romans 11:7–8

a: and I heal them
t: "And I heal them": a future verb
p: The last verb is future in Greek: "and I will heal them." Some read a door left open at the very end.
b: After "so that they never" (mēpote), Greek usually uses the subjunctive, but the last verb is future indicative: iasomai, "I will heal." Matthew's quotation has the same form, and the Plain follows Matthew's "and turn, and I heal them." Some interpreters take the future as a quiet promise: if they turn, God will heal. Others think it is simply the Septuagint's grammar and carries no special meaning. Either way the healing Isaiah held out is still God's to give.

a: this salvation from God has been sent out to the Gentiles
p: The third time Paul turns to the Gentiles (13:46; 18:6). Is this a final verdict on the Jewish people, or not?
b: Paul has turned to the Gentiles twice before, at Pisidian Antioch (13:46) and Corinth (18:6), and both times went back to the synagogue in the next city. Now the book ends. Some scholars (Haenchen, J. T. Sanders) read 28:28 as Luke's final word: the Jews have refused, and the future belongs to the Gentile church. Others (Jervell, Tannehill) note that some Jews believed (28:24), that Paul goes on welcoming "everyone" (28:30), and that Luke tells a tragedy, not a rejection: the open ending leaves the story of Israel unfinished. Joseph Tyson finds Luke ambivalent. Christian use of this verse to teach that God had rejected the Jews is part of a painful history (see the card).

a: this salvation from God
p: A rare Greek word, sōtērion, that Luke uses only at the start of his Gospel and here at the end of Acts.
b: The neuter noun sōtērion, "salvation," appears in Luke-Acts only three times: Simeon, holding the baby Jesus, says, "with my own eyes I have seen your salvation" (Luke 2:30); John the Baptist's preaching ends with the Septuagint's "all flesh will see the salvation of God" (Luke 3:6, from Isaiah 40:5; the Hebrew there reads only "and all flesh will see it," Isaiah 40:5); and here. The two volumes are framed by the same word. Psalm 67 had prayed that God's salvation be known "among all nations" (Psalm 67:2). What Simeon saw in the temple now goes out to the Gentiles from Rome.
orig: τοῦτο τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ (touto to sōtērion tou theou)
r: Luke 2:30–32; Luke 3:6; Isaiah 40:5; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 52:10; Psalm 67:2; Psalm 98:3

a: in quarters he paid for himself
p: En idiō misthōmati can mean "at his own expense" or "in his own rented lodging." Both may be true.
b: Misthōma usually means a price paid for hire or rent. So the phrase can mean "at his own expense" (Paul supported himself, perhaps by his trade, perhaps with gifts like the one from Philippi, Philippians 4:18) or "in his own rented quarters" (KJV "in his own hired house"). The setting of 28:16–23, with visitors coming to his lodging, fits either. The point is that Paul, though a prisoner, had a home of a sort, open to all comers.

a: For two full years
p: Acts does not say what happened next. Early tradition says Paul was released, preached further, and died under Nero.
b: Luke stops at "two full years," which suggests he knew the custody ended. Some scholars, Ramsay among them, suggested the case lapsed when no accusers came; Sherwin-White doubted that any such rule existed. Early Christian writers say more. 1 Clement (about 96) says Paul taught righteousness to the whole world, reached "the limit of the west" and bore witness before rulers (1 Clement 5:5–7); Paul had planned to go to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28), and the Muratorian Fragment mentions that journey. Eusebius (Church History 2.22; 2.25) reports a release, further travel, a second imprisonment and Paul's beheading in Rome under Nero, and the Acts of Paul tells his martyrdom. Many scholars doubt the release and think Paul died at the end of these two years.
r: 20:25; 20:38; Romans 15:24; Romans 15:28; Philippians 1:19–26; 2 Timothy 4:6–8; 2 Timothy 4:16–17; 1 Clement 5:5–7

a: and no one stopped him
p: Acts ends on akōlytōs, "without hindrance," a legal word. The prisoner is chained; the message is not.
b: The very last word of Acts is akōlytōs, "without hindrance," a term found in legal papyri for something done without obstruction. Paul is in chains, but the word goes out freely, "with complete freedom to speak" (parrēsia, frank and open speech), the gift the believers prayed for in 4:29. 2 Timothy says it the same way: "God's word is not in chains" (2 Timothy 2:9). The Plain ends with "no one stopped him" so that, as in Luke's Greek, the book closes on freedom.
orig: μετὰ πάσης παρρησίας ἀκωλύτως (meta pasēs parrēsias akōlytōs)
